utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One matter, Mr. Brown, before we proceed. You and I are speaking the same language. There are interpreters between us. So if you can pause before you give your answer and I will do the same and that will facilitate the interpretation. And if you could try to deliberately speak at a slightly slower pace than you might normally do so, then we shouldn't have any problems. Now, for the purposes of the record, your name is Ewan Brown; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you were born on the 15th of May of 1964?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you are a British citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are currently employed as a military analyst within the Office of the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have a bachelor's degree in history from the University of East Anglia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And you have a master's degree in criminology from the University of Leicester?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You attended the role military academy Sandhurst in 1986; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that, I believe, is the officer training college or academy for officers commissioned into the British army; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If at this point, Your Honour, we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are now, Mr. Brown, a military analyst within the Office of the Prosecutor. Can you explain to the Judges the role of the military analyst within the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a small team of military analysts within the Office of the Prosecutor who sit somewhat separately from the investigative teams and the Prosecution teams. The role of the analysts, military analysts, is to provide specialist military assistance and analysis, the analysis of documentation or evidence, in order to synthesise, analyse, and collect that material, invariably on a military-related issue, with which either to assist the investigation process or, during the Prosecution phase, to assist the Prosecution in making sense of the military component of the former Yugoslavia and the issues we're dealing with in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When did you come to the Office of the Prosecutor to work as a military analyst?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you've been working on material within the office since that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Your Honour, I could offer into evidence the witness's curriculum vitae, and if that could be given an exhibit number, and if that document to be placed under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be S339, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown if you could please have in front of you your report dated the 18th of July, 2002. I've just got a few preliminary questions before we start discussing that report. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, this report entitled "Military developments Prijedor municipality 1991 to 1992, a background report," who asked you to produce this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The legal team on this case asked me to compile this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Specifically whom on the legal team asked you to produce this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner asked me to produce the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When were you asked to produce this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning of this year I was provisionally made aware that I may -- or a report, a military analysis report may be required in relation to this case, although I was not formally tasked to write the report until May of this year. At the beginning of May, I was, as I said, asked to compile a report relating to the military issues in the Prijedor municipality during the spring and summer months of 1992 in particular. After a short period of preliminary study, in the middle of May there was a formal meeting at which the structure of the report was outlined by myself to the legal team, and really from the middle of May this year until the report's completion date, which I believe is the 18th of July was when I compiled the report itself, I believe a draft may have been ready around the end of June, but the report was completed in July this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What instructions were you given by Ms. Korner, by the legal team, in respect of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The instruction was somewhat general. I was asked to look at the military component, military activities in Prijedor municipality, in particular, in the spring and summer months 1992, in order to paint a picture of which military units were present in the municipality and their conduct. After my preliminary study and when we met again, I stated that the report should be somewhat expanded in some areas, and relating to other -- some wider issues that did have a bearing on Prijedor but may not necessarily have been evident when we first discussed it in early May. So I was in a position to, in essence, influence the structure of the report, its content, and I was not guided or hampered in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm right in saying that this report is based exclusively on documentary material; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what documentary material you have relied upon in producing this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the material really can be categorised, I suppose, into four areas. The first category are military documents in the possession of the OTP. Those documents, in particular, come from the 1st Krajina Corps, JNA 5th Corps, 1st Krajina Corps, which was the corps that existed in the Krajina area, Bosnian Krajina area, during the period of our concern, although there are a number of other military documents that are of relevance. The second are police documents, again relating either to the wider Krajina or, more specifically, to Prijedor municipality. The third category are political or governmental-style documents, either relating directly to Prijedor or to the regional level in Banja Luka, and a number relating to the republic level. The fourth category are a small number, relatively small number, of open-source documents: Press articles, and I believe there's one video. Again, that's as an open-source document. So the military police political and open-source are the four categories of documents that I've used.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've stated to the Court that this report is principally a report concerned with military events. Why have you therefore included documents relating to the police, political documents, and open-source material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of those document make reference to military matters, military events, or, I would argue, influenced the deployment of military forces in Prijedor in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many documents are referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I have some 260-odd footnotes, although a number of documents are referenced on a number of -- throughout -- or duplicated, replicated through the report. Some of the footnotes are comments by myself and not actually reference documents. I believe there are around 150 individual documents in total with reference to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who selected those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I don't want this next question, I don't want to sort of number by number, but could you explain to the Judges where proportionately those documents come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents themselves come from an array of sources. The open-source documents I've already discussed are newspaper articles in the public domain. The other documents come either from seizures that the OTP has carried out in a number of locations in the Krajina, documents provided by the Bosnia-Herzegovina government authorities. I believe there's one document which has come from the Republic of Croatia, and a small number of documents which are provided by the Republika Srpska authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where do the majority of the documents that you've relied upon come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately three-quarters, I believe, of the documents that I used were from OTP seizures, either seizures that too place in Banja Luka or seizures that took place in Prijedor municipality. I think the figure is round about three-quarters of those documents were seized documents by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So we can say that approximately 75 per cent of the documents that you relied upon were seized directly from the Bosnian Serb army and Bosnian Serb authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that's approximately the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you give the Judges some idea of, taken together all of these documents, their integrity as a source in producing your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documentation that I utilised here, a significant section comes from seized material, in essence, primary-source material that the OTP obtained. I believe that those documents are genuine and reflect -- and contemporary and reflect the picture contained within them. The documents that were provided through other means, such as those through the Bosnian authorities, which I have used, I have tried to utilise documents that are corroborated by other sources or -- and by that I mean corroborated by the seized documents, or were, if I put the seized documents together with documents that have been obtained through, say, the Bosnian authorities, that they can be corroborated, I believe. I believe the documents to be accurate. I'm not a forensic document specialist, but when the documents are put together, I believe that they are credible and reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, on page 3 of your report, you state that there are certain limitations contained within this report. It's broadly referred to in paragraph 3. Can you state to the Judges what you believe are the limitations of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The report does have certain limitations which I wanted to just introduce at the introduction of the document. The report is not an exhaustive study of every single document relating to Prijedor municipality. That would be, I think, a bit of a physical impossibility to go through every single document. So there is just a physical limitation there. The report is documentary based. It is not a report that contains information relating to witness testimony or any other material outside written -- the written documentation I've seen. So there's a limitation there. The report is limited in time. It relates predominantly to the spring and summer months of 1992, although it does touch on issues in late 1991, but it is limited in time. And it is limited to some extent in location. This is a report about Prijedor municipality. Prijedor was not an isolated municipality within the Krajina and Bosnia generally, but this is about Prijedor and is not about necessarily all other areas. So that is also a limitation. I think those are some of the areas that I believe should be taken into consideration when reading the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If, Mr. President, the report could be given an exhibit number and then I think we can move ahead with the heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The exhibit number would be S340. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do object, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have two reasons for the objection. Number 1, we believe that because of the limitations as Mr. Brown has outlined for us, the report cannot give us and will not give us a complete and thorough analysis required, based upon the indictment that's been charged against Dr. Stakic and based upon his experience in connection with reviewing this and creating this report. Secondly, it is rather clear that Mr. Brown is simply an employee of the OTP who has generated this report in a subjective manner and is clearly, pursuant to the instruction of the lead trial attorney, Joanna Korner, has prepared a report looking at a very limited scope, in his own words and a very narrow focus-minded report of the events in Prijedor and making an attempt to try to link them with the accused. Clearly in his direct -- thus far direct examination, he has outlined for us that he is a military analyst and that he was providing some military overviews. The report, however, is more expansive than that and attempts, inadequately, in our opinion, to connect a political individual as charged in the indictment to any military actions. And as a subcategory of that, Mr. Brown has clearly indicated in his direct that he did not go beyond the region, and yet he attempts to give us some sort of opinion in connection with command structure and hierarchy but does not go beyond the Prijedor municipality or the events prior to the spring and summer of 1992 or those events subsequent to that. Interestingly enough, we received this morning in excess of 250 pages under the ambit of Rule 68, which, not surprising to the Defence, involve specifically the area where Mr. Brown claims to have reviewed documents, namely, the 1st Krajina Corps, documents from the 5th Kozara Brigade, and documents from the 434th Motorised Brigade. Those documents were not included in his analysis, clearly, because we're receiving them not only on the eve of his testimony but on the day of his testimony. I think it's highly prejudicial and it's something that the Office of the Prosecutor knew about since these seizures occurred in 1997, that it should be disallowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want to hear me, or ... I mean, I -- in essence, I've distilled from what my learned friend has said two objections. He objects to the report based on the limitations that the witness has stated. I mean, I think it's perfectly fair for any witness to openly express to Judges that there are certain limitations within a report. The Judges should know about that. And that doesn't mean to say that a witness should be precluded from testifying or producing his report before this Chamber. Secondly, as regards an individual being an employee of the OTP, I think it's standard practice in many countries that certain expert or professional witnesses who are employed by a prosecution office or by a police authority testify on a daily basis before courts, and they are certainly never accused of being biased or partial. Equally, in this institution it has been a regular practice for employees who have worked for either the military analysis team or the leadership research team to testify before chambers. Of course, it is a matter for you ultimately to decide whether or not a witness is biased or not, but I don't think that that is an objection which should preclude him from being heard. And ultimately, the only way whether or not you can actually judge whether Mr. Ostojic is correct in what he is saying is to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber rejects the objections by the Defence. It would be premature to rule on the probative value of this report before having heard the report. Of course, we are aware to a certain extent what we will hear, but, as we did it earlier, the final evaluation of evidence is for the Judges, and the documents presented as such in principle are admitted into evidence, and therefore this document is admitted into evidence as S340. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, my understanding is that you have created a PowerPoint presentation for the purposes of your evidence here today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I know the report is somewhat lengthy and I felt maybe the easiest way to synthesize some of the key issues was to put it into a PowerPoint presentation, which I hope works.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The PowerPoint presentation is, in effect, an abbreviation of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you have hard copies of that presentation before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is also a French version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if you could open your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're going to be using documents and also viewing the PowerPoint presentation, and if you see on the panel before you, you have buttons marked "computer evidence" and "video evidence." "Computer evidence" will give you the PowerPoint presentation and when the witness places a document that he's used in support of an assertion that he's making, if you switch to "video evidence," that will give you the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, this first slide marked "JNA command structure," could you explain this slide to the Judges, in particular, how it's relevant to Prijedor? And if you could use the pointer, I think that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the pointer, unfortunately, is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll look at that in the break, but if you could explain this particular slide to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the first parts of the report deals with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we can't see anything on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Have you pressed the button, Your Honour, marked "computer evidence" on the panel in front of you? And it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All of the screens are silent. It's really dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mine has gone exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's blue. Okay. There's only one screen not working, the one of Judge Vassylenko. But you can start. We have the possibility to follow on one computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could explain this slide to the Court, please, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first part of the report deals with general developments and outlines some of the military units that are relevant to Prijedor and to the Krajina area. And what I wanted to do here on this slide was to synthesize the command structure of the JNA Yugoslav National Army prior to the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Army in May 1992. The JNA command structure in Bosnia comprised of a military district which was located in Sarajevo, the 2nd Military District. To all intents and purposes, the 2nd military district covered the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was established in the early part of 1992, in part due to the withdrawal of JNA forces from Croatia. The 2nd military district consisted of a number of corps. The 5th Corps, the JNA 5th Corps, was one of those corps, and it was located in Banja Luka, and that is the second box, subordinated to the 2nd military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I be so impolite to interrupt you? When you address certain periods in time, could you please be more concrete for the purposes of our trial? When you, for example, state "in the early part of 1992," could you be a little bit more concrete?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I have an input on this, Your Honour? And also, since Mr. Cayley was kind enough to suggest, and Mr. Brown agreed, can he also direct us to the document so that we can follow where it is that he claims that it was established in 1992, if we may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think first of all we leave it -- we should leave it to the OTP and to the witness himself to direct us if he so wants. If there are any problems, then no doubt it's for the Defence, or later the Judges, to ask some questions. But no doubt it would be helpful that we don't have to do this exercise three times, that immediately, where necessary, the sources could be mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just mention the issue that Mr. Ostojic has just raised. Obviously there are 150 documents in this report and we don't anticipate referring to every single document, otherwise we are going to be here for weeks. I think there are certain issues, such as the existence of the 2nd military district, which, quite frankly, if that's challenged, I'd be surprised. So we have selected 30 documents. Mr. Ostojic has all of the documents. If he wants to put them to the witness in his cross-examination, he can do so. But we don't intend to produce documents for every single assertion that is made here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply. If they claim that it was established in 1992, they have the burden of proof. Let them prove it. We contest that. It's absolutely incorrect. Mr. Brown knows it's incorrect, Mr. Cayley knows it's incorrect. The OTP in other cases have established that it's incorrect. If they are going to tell this Court, we're going to throw everything at you and let's see if the Defence and the Defence counsel can somehow manoeuvre through these land mines that we set up for them. It's just simply not true. I cannot, as an official of the Court and as an attorney representing the accused Dr. Stakic, allow this witness to tell us something and claim that there's any veracity to his report when there's no basis for him to establish whatsoever that this 2nd military district in Sarajevo was established for the first time in 1992. It's just simply not true. I can't allow it to happen, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. But I think we should calm down and return to the language normally used in this courtroom, and I would advise you not to tell a witness that he knows that it's incorrect what he states here in the courtroom. I think it's not necessary to go down to such a level. As I had emphasised, it would be of assistance to be more concrete with the dates, and if you, Mr. Brown, or the counsel of the OTP regards as necessary, please give us a hint on what basis you come to the conclusion. Thank you. But the initial point of this dispute was a question: What do you mean by "the beginning of 1992"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm unaware of the exact establishment date of the 2nd Military District. I believe the 2nd Military District was established as part of the wider agreements in relation to the settlement of the war in Croatia. Part of that agreement included the withdrawal of forces from Croatia in late 1991, I believe in December 1991 was when the agreement was signed, although I do not know the exact date. I believe - and I don't know if -- I don't think I've referenced it in this report - the 2nd Military District was established either in the last few days of 1991 or the first few days of 1992. Prior to the 2nd Military District, the units in Bosnia had been, in essence, commanded by the 1st Military District in Belgrade, which has headquarters in Belgrade. So the 2nd Military District was a new establishment structure. I know from other documentation, some of which we will show later, that the 2nd Military District was in establishment in the early months of 1992, that daily combat reports from the JNA 5th Corps in Banja Luka were being sent to the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo, and there are references in my report to that effect. Without going through each individual footnote, I cannot highlight the first daily combat report that I can show to you that the 2nd Military District was in establishment, but I know, for example, that we have a reference on the 17th of February, 1992, which is a daily combat report to the 2nd Military District, showing that it certainly was in establishment by that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the next box down in your command structure is the 5th Corps in Banja Luka. Were there other corps that were under the command of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of other corps the 2nd Military District commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why have you highlighted the 5th Corps in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA 5th Corps in Banja Luka in essence, its peacetime location covered the municipality of Prijedor, as well as other municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina area. So the 5th Corps was the corps that covered -- included Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And again we'll see a number of documents, I think later on, from that corps. But the next question I have for you is the next box which is formed by a dotted line is the Prijedor regional command. What can you tell us about that as a military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor municipality there existed a Prijedor garrison, a peacetime garrison headquarters. At some stage in 1992, the JNA 5th Corps established the Prijedor Regional Command, which in essence was more of an operational command. It sat between two brigades and the corps. I do not know the exact establishment date of the Prijedor Regional Command, but I do know that it was established -- it had been established at least by the 10th of May, 1992 because of documentation, and I believe there's some footnotes in my report which I can draw your attention to. I also know that on the 17th of February, from documentation, 1992, there was a move and an instruction from the 5th Corps to collocate the Territorial Defence in Prijedor, the Territorial Defence headquarters, with the command headquarters, that is, the JNA command headquarters in Prijedor, and I would assess that sometime between February 1992 and May 1992 the 5th Corps established Prijedor Regional Command. Prijedor -- and the reason I put the box in dotted line is because I don't know when the establishment -- the exact establishment date of that regional command was. The JNA 5th Corps established a number of subordinate commands in between the brigades of the corps throughout 1992, and Prijedor Regional Command was one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the two brigades that you have underneath Prijedor Regional Command, geographically, where were those two brigades located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both brigades were located in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, again, when do you know -- and again, this may only be a sort of by the latest date -- were those two brigades under the command of the JNA 5th Corps and in existence? What documentary evidence have you seen of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both the 343rd Motorised Brigade and the 5th Kozara Brigade, sometimes known as the 5th Infantry Brigade, were mobilised in September 1991 for operations in Croatia. In September 1991, I believe on the 18th of September. The JNA 5th Corps received an order to conduct operations in Croatia to defeat Croatian paramilitary units and to assist in protecting JNA facilities in Croatia, and its instruction was to, in essence, head for the Hungarian border through Western Slavonia. Both the 343rd Motorised Brigade and the 5th infantry or 5th Kozara Brigade were mobilised as parts of that operation and deployed to western Slavonia in September 1991 and became or were under the control of the corps from that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I already now ask you whether or not this 343rd Motorised Brigade ever had another name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the JNA transformed into the VRS in Bosnia, they dropped the first 3 and called it the 43rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, these two brigades, very briefly, did they see action in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Both brigades did see action in Croatia. Elements of both brigades were deployed to Croatia from September 1991, and elements of the brigades remained in western Slavonia I believe until about June 1992. There was a period of rotation where elements of the brigade would go back to Prijedor on leave, and some documentary evidence indicates that that occurred, but both brigades saw combat action in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you say in this document that the commander of the 343rd Motorised Brigade was Vladimir Arsic and the deputy was Radmilo Zeljaja. You also indicate that the commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade was Pero Colic. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are a number of documents, including some referenced in my report, indicating the positions of these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move now, please, to the next slide, which deals with the Territorial Defence structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to Their Honours the distinction between the JNA and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both the JNA and the Territorial Defence, or TO, were a component of what was known as All People's Defence in the former Yugoslavia. This, in essence, was a process by where the country could be defended in times of attack. It included the mobilisation of personnel at municipal and local level into the Territorial Defence, providing a more localised defensive structure, whilst the JNA's function was primarily to defend the federal borders. The Territorial Defence was based on each individual republic. It was a republic-level organisation funded by each republic, and with a republic Territorial Defence staff in each of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, dealing first of all with the three boxes that run down the middle of the chart, labelled "Republic TO staff, District TO staff, Banja Luka TO Prijedor," can you explain that line of command to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, there were various command staffs within the Territorial Defence. There was a republic TO staff in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was based in Sarajevo. Subordinate to that were a number of district Territorial Defence staffs, including one in Banja Luka that covered a number of the Krajina municipalities, including Prijedor. Subordinate to the District TO staffs were those municipal Territorial Defence units based on a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the TO in Prijedor was not the only municipal Territorial Defence under the command of the District TO staff in Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I believe there are a large number of municipalities in the Krajina that also fell under the command of the District TO in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the district and republican Territorial Defence staff, were they staffed in part by regular JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, to now address the broken lines that you have going between the District TO staff in Banja Luka to the 5th Corps in Banja Luka, can you explain the meaning of that broken line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I put in these lines and links because it's clear from documentation that the 5th Corps had a significant influence on the District TO staff in Banja Luka, in part due to operations in Croatia in late 1991, when a number of Territorial Defence units, Territorial Defence units were mobilised for operations, including the 5th Kozara Brigade. The 5th Kozara Brigade and one other Territorial Defence-based unit were placed under the command of the 5th Corps for operations in Croatia. But also in the spring months of 1992, as the situation in Bosnia developed and changed, the 5th Corps began issuing instructions to the District TO staff in Banja Luka, and those instructions were being disseminated down to municipal bodies. So although there was this republic district municipality command chain, the 5th Corps, by April 1992, was issuing instructions to the District TO staff on a variety of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you also have a box linking the Territorial Defence in Prijedor with the JNA Prijedor regional command. You also have a broken line there. What does that broken line signify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, some documentation indicates that Prijedor Regional Command was in a position of some influence on the TO in Prijedor. I mentioned the 17th of February instruction whereby there was a collocation -- to be a collocation of the TO headquarters with the JNA command in Prijedor. In May 1992 there were a number of instructions coming -- one, for example, which I think I've referenced, whereby the 5th Corps requested from the Regional Command the disposition of units within Prijedor, including Territorial Defence units down to platoon squads, and other documentation linking and involving meetings indicate that the Prijedor Regional Command had an influence on the Territorial Defence in Prijedor. And ultimately when the TO was finally disbanded in late May 1992, the Territorial Defence commander was subordinated to the Prijedor Regional Command and the conscripts were disseminated into units including the 43rd Motorised Brigade. So I believe there was a clear link between the Prijedor Regional Command and the TO in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the final box is the link between the Prijedor municipal government and the TO in Prijedor, and again you have a broken line. Can you indicate the significance of that particular linkage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More generally, the municipalities had a significant role to play with the Territorial Defence in a municipality. Territorial Defence commanders would be nominated at municipal level, although they would have to be authorised through the Territorial Defence command chain. Issues relating to financing, mobilisation, records, were within the remit of the Prijedor municipal government. And again, documentation, specifically relating to Prijedor, in late May, shows that, for example, the Crisis Staff authorised the disbandment of the TO and the placing of the TO commander within the Prijedor regional command. So again, this linkage into the TO is highlighted on this slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I think this particular subject-matter is contained in page 8 to 12 of your report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, here you are showing the Bosnian Serb army command structure. First of all, when did the VSR, the Bosnian Serb army, form in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the 12th of May in Banja Luka, there was a meeting held, the 16th assembly session of the Serb Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, at which an announcement was made to establish the Bosnian Serb army, initially called the army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, latterly called the VRS, sometimes referred to as the Bosnian Serb army. Decisions were taken at that meeting on the 12th of May establishing the army and establishing Ratko Mladic as its commander, or commander of the Main Staff. There was a period whereby there was a formal transition between the remaining JNA units in Bosnia and the establishment of the VRS, and on the 19th, 20th of May, 1992, was when JNA units were meant to have left Bosnia, but in essence there was a transformation of those JNA units into the new Bosnian Serb army. But the establishment date of the army was the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, looking specifically at the chart, you have, in the position of the Supreme Command of the Bosnian Serb army the presidency of the Bosnian Serb Republic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The 12th of May decision made it clear that the presidency was the highest organ and was in command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, underneath that you have the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army, and you've noted that that headquarters was formerly the 2nd Military District that you've already referred to, the 2nd Military District of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, elements of the 2nd Military District in essence formed the nucleus of the VSR or VRS Main Staff. For example, Ratko Mladic had been initially appointed to be deputy commander of the 2nd Military District. He was then laterally appointed to commander of the military -- 2nd Military District. But he was appointed as commander of the VRS Main Staff at the 12th of May, and a number of other officers who were at the 2nd Military District remained and formed a nucleus of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It may assist if you could immediately mention this document of 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe it's footnote 25 in the report. I have a copy of the report, the document, if there are particular sections that need to be referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be of assistance if this document could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We are going to refer to sections of the document, Your Honour. It's a voluminous document, but I'm perfectly prepared to tender all of it as an exhibit if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to this later. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will bear that in mind. We anticipate looking at a section of it, so what I can do, in order to meet your concerns, is introduce another part of it which deals with this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Footnote 25, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, you then note in this military command structure underneath the Main Staff the 1st Krajina Corps. Now, first question: Were there a number of corps that were subordinated to the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of other corps. I believe initially five, and it grew to six by the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the main headquarters of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps's main headquarters was in Banja Luka; however, it had, as a result of operations in Croatia in 1991 and into 1992, deployed a headquarters to Stara Gradiska, which is north of Banja Luka over the river in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the 1st Krajina Corps headquarters was based on the nucleus of the JNA 5th Corps headquarters in Banja Luka; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. A significant number of the officers who were serving, if you like, as 5th Corps officers simply remained and stayed in their positions when they named -- the name changed to the 1st Krajina Corps. And the Corps Commander, for example, General -- Major General Momir Talic, who was appointed commander in May -- March 1992 remained as the 1st Krajina Corps commander through the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've noted underneath that, as with the previous slide, that there was an intermediate headquarters between the brigades and the 1st Krajina Corps, that being the Prijedor Regional Command and we won't go into that because you've already explained that. But underneath that command were two brigades: The 43rd Motorised Brigade and the 5th Kozara Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The command structure stayed the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And as you previously responded to Judge Schomburg's question, the 343rd Brigade of the JNA simply became the 43rd Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the box on the right-hand side I'd like you to explain where you state -- and you've already touched on this issue, that Territorial Defence units that had previously operated to another chain of command were integrated into the Bosnian Serb army. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, again at the 16th assembly session on the 12th of May it was announced that Territorial Defence units should be integrated and become part of the Bosnian Serb army, and that process was put into action relatively quickly. Territorial Defence units were often renamed as light infantry brigades and were integrated into the relevant corps of the VRS, and in Prijedor municipality, by late May 1992, in accordance with the direction that had been given on the 12th of May, the TO of Prijedor was integrated into the 1st Krajina Corps. The TO commander, Slobodan Kuruzovic was placed under the command of the Prijedor regional command, and from other documentation from the 1st Krajina Corps, a similar process occurred in a number of other municipalities in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I believe that this is covered in pages 10 to 14 of your report. If you can just check that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The elements of that are contained in those sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now move to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you believe you can do it in the next five minutes or would it be appropriate --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it might bleed over 11.00, Your Honour, to be honest. I think it might take a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's have a break now. The trial stays adjourned now until 11.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I just ask one thing of the witness because I can't talk to him in the break, if he could pull out the section of the assembly minutes about the formation of the Bosnian Serb army that you were interested in yourself, if he could do that in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. This would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, this slide is I think an abbreviated representation of pages 15 and 16 of your written report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain what this slide represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to simplify the issues relating to the SDS takeover of Prijedor municipality on the 30th of April, 1992, highlighting, where I could, where the documents indicated participants, where military support was given, and the reporting that went through the JNA 5th Corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, looking at the extreme right-hand side of this slide, you have "Reporting: 5th Corps informed reported to 2nd Military District 1 May 1992." If you could take the first document that you selected and place that on the ELMO. First of all, Mr. Brown, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is an example of the daily combat reports that the JNA 5th Corps would send to the 2nd military district command. These daily combat reports were normally sent once a day, sometimes twice a day, and on rare occasions three times a day, in the documents I've seen in 1992. And this is in essence a standard daily combat report with a standard format, and it is the 5th Corps reporting key issues up to the 2nd military district command on the 1st of May, 1992. I'd like to draw your attention in particular to paragraph 1 and the sentence which is highlighted, which states: "After the SDS takeover in Prijedor, the situation in general is calm. During the night, a killing occurred at a checkpoint in Prijedor and a Muslim organisation sealed off the village of Kozarac, preventing access to it." For me, this indicates a knowledge on behalf of the JNA 5th Corps of the events in Prijedor, and in particular, the takeover in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the original Serbian version of this document, who is the document signed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document -- the signature block is "Major General Momir Talic," but it's signed on his behalf I believe by Dragan Marticic who was chief of operations and training at the headquarters of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if we can go back to your slide. Now, immediately to the left of the box that you have marked "reporting" you have a box marked "military support," and underneath that Lieutenant Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja. Can you explain that conclusion that you reached in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, if it's possible just to go back slightly to the reporting issue. When I say 5th Corps informed, there is a reference in a 5th Corps daily duty team, basically a notebook of the 5th Corps, dated the 30th of April, indicating that the SDS had taken control of Prijedor, and I believe that that reference was used as the basis for the reference in the daily combat report of the 1st of May that annotated notebook reference is footnote 51 in the report. Moving on to the second box -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you? May I ask the OTP: What about these documents mentioned here? How do you want to tender or not to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, our intention was not to offer every single document, because I think that will create a situation of information overload. If you wish, for certain documents to be tendered which we're not tendering, I'm perfectly prepared to do that, but it was only my intention to offer the document of the 1st of May of 1992 which was on the ELMO, just to allow the witness to refer to the notebook, which he has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in this trial, normally we attach immediately a new exhibit number. This would be then 341. Do you have copies available for all participants?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that everybody has a copy in front of them already of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thanks. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll remember that in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Exhibit S341. And then, finally, it would be of assistance that immediately if reference is made to footnotes - for example, footnote 25, in part indeed it was Exhibit 141-1-2 whenever you mention a footnote, it could be of assistance that we could hear immediately whether or not this document was already admitted into evidence, and I think you just made reference to footnote 52. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe footnote 51, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 51, yes. Duty team notebook entry. I think such a notebook entry, if it's not yet admitted, it would be of assistance if this could -- such a document could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can arrange that, Your Honour. I just need to sort that one out. We'll do that in the break and come back to it. But certainly for those documents that we do intend to put into evidence, we have noted where they are existing exhibits so that we don't put repeat documents into the document file. But I can sort that out in the break, that particular document, and bring Mr. Brown back to the particular reference that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, moving back to the slide, issue of military support, can you explain that part of the slide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There is some limited evidence that the military were involved prior to the takeover in encouraging and supporting the takeover, and I found a reference to a radio interview - a Radio Prijedor interview - later in the war in 1995, at which Simo Miskovic, Slobodan Kuruzovic, who was the Territorial Defence commander, and Simo Drljaca appeared. In the transcript of that radio interview, Miskovic and Kuruzovic indicated that there had been a meeting at the barracks in Prijedor at which support and encouragement was given by Colonel Arsic, Prijedor regional commander and also commander of the 343rd Brigade. That is referenced in my report on page 15. Kuruzovic in the transcript stated that they went up to the barracks to discuss military tactics and decide when and what had to be done. Dr. Stakic, former president of the municipality, myself - meaning Kuruzovic - Drljaca, Jankovic, Cadjo, Miskovic, as chairman of the SDS, and Lieutenant Colonel Arsic, was there. He went on to say that they discussed nearly up to 7.00 and upon the colonel's insistence, decided that the moment was right, in essence, to carry out the takeover. Miskovic also stated a similar event, description of the events in his -- during the same radio interview, that in essence Colonel Arsic encouraged them and gave them support and that they had a good chance of success.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just remind us again - I know you've already said it - who was Major Zeljaja. You've already said that Lieutenant Colonel Arsic was the commander of the 343rd Brigade, later the 43rd Brigade. Who was Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljaja was deputy commander of the 43rd Motorised Brigade, he later became commander of the brigade, later, I believe in August 1992. Zeljaja, also in a quoted newspaper article in Kozarski Vjesnik in 1994 echoed to some extent that military support had been given, and in that interview, Zeljaja was quoted as saying they had offered maximal help and support to the SDS, both in organising preparation and advising them in order to overcome certain problems in relation to the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, you quote this in a footnote or where can we find this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Zeljaja interview is at footnote 50, Your Honour, which is a Kozarski Vjesnik article dated the 20th of May, 1994, entitled "We know our goal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document as such would be available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I always have to ask: It's included in this file on exhibits? Because it's now in a totally different order than it was today -- as it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said a moment ago, my original intention was not to offer all 150 documents, for the obvious reasons. That document was originally disclosed as part of the footnotes but was not in the bundle. It's not something I intend to offer to the Court. If you want us to, we can do so, but the problem is going to be that Mr. Brown is going to take a long, long time to get through all of this if we put into evidence every single document that's referred to in his report. So what we tried to do was select what we thought were the most relevant documents. But as you wish. If you want us to put it in, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary that it's done in the presence of the witness, only if by the end of the day or in the beginning of tomorrow, also for the purposes that it may serve for the cross-examination, it is available for the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I think also the Defence should immediately tell us if they need a document as such, and not only in the form of a footnote. Please, I can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document that I think Mr. Brown is referencing in footnote 50 has already been admitted into evidence under number S274A and B, over our objection, but nonetheless admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are discussing now only the radio interview; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Actually, specifically the article that was just referenced, "We know your goal," interview with Colonel Zeljaja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I recall your objections. And we wanted to come back to the one or other, and therefore my question is now, because we didn't decide on this, we wanted to decide in the presence of Witness Brown. So let us proceed, but have the documents mentioned by either the Chamber or the Defence available until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So just to be clear, Mr. President, all of those documents to which the witness refers but which are not immediately available to put on the ELMO, we'll deal with those tomorrow, essentially, as part of the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it's necessary to have it once again as part of the examination-in-chief. We have heard it now. But to allow us later on, if the document is contested - and as we just heard, one of the documents was highly disputed, and especially this radio statement - and therefore please provide us with the underlying document. We will draw your attention to these documents that we believe are necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the left-hand side of the slide, you have there "participants." Now, my assumption is that here you're referring to the participants in the takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if you could please place on the ELMO document of the 30th of April, which I think you have in the binder in front of you. Now, first of all, could you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a Prijedor SJB document dated the 30th of April, which was sent to the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, and it's the SJB chief, Simo Drljaca, in essence, giving a summary of events on the takeover. It reads: "Based on your dispatch of the above number and date, please be informed of the following: Ten police stations and 1.587 policemen were mobilised. No one failed to respond or avoided work duty. In accordance with the conclusions of the executive board of the Serbian assembly of Prijedor municipality, at 0400 hours in the municipality, control was seized over SJB's and all other major facilities. These activities were carried out in a synchronised manner and without firing a bullet. Normal work and operation of the service was established through guarding, policing, and patrol services. Industrial and other organisations are operating normally. You will receive timely information on future activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you conclude from this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When this document is placed alongside the interview, it's clear that the police were heavily involved in the takeover, and according to this document, that the takeover was carried out in accordance with the conclusions of an executive board of the Serb assembly in Prijedor and that power was taken -- or control was taken without firing a round.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Where does this document come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was seized by the OTP in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you also conclude that TO, or Territorial Defence, forces were participants, from your slide. I think you've already touched upon this regarding the radio interview. How do you conclude that the TO were involved in the takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is some limited information based on that radio interview from Kuruzovic, who stated that he and subordinate officers had drawn up a plan and mobilised certain TO personnel, and together with the police, they took over key buildings and facilities in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could move on, please, Mr. Brown, to the next slide. Your Honour, if I could offer the document that's just been referred to as S342, please. That's the document dated the 30th of April, 1992 from Prijedor public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I first ask Madam Registrar whether or not this document was already admitted earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It has a 65 ter number of 105, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Under the reservation that it must be double-checked, objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, this slide entitled "strategic goals," to what does this refer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This refers to discussions that took place at the 16th assembly session on the 12th of May in Banja Luka, the meeting that I alluded to earlier on, which also took decisions in establishing the Bosnian Serb army. This meeting, in essence, was a meeting of the senior SDS leadership, including the republic-level leadership, Krajisnik, Karadzic, as well as municipal leaders. At this meeting, Radovan Karadzic announced the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs and listed them in priority order. The session also adopted a number of other decisions, including the establishment of the army and the appointment of Ratko Mladic as its commander, or commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an existing exhibit within the case. It's S141-1, minutes of the 16th session of the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brown, I know you've extracted a part of that existing exhibit for the purposes of this slide, and if you could place that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in the English version, Your Honours, this is pages 13, 14, and 15 of Prosecutor's Exhibit S141, so it doesn't need to be re-exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence whether or not Dr. Stakic has this document in a language he understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll have to ask him, Your Honour. If you could just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. Because if not, I would appreciate that the highlighted sentences should be read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for the courtesy. We do have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could read out the first goal and then what I'd like you to do is go back to the slide and explain your interpretation of that goal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karadzic announced the goals and in the minutes stated: "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the president, the government, council for national security, which we have set up and formulated, have formulated the strategic priorities, that is to say, the strategic goals, for the Serbian people. The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities, separation of states, separation from those who are our enemies, who have used every opportunity, especially this century, to attack us, and would continue with such practices if we were to stay together in the same state." This strategic goal was placed as the first strategic goal, and there are references later in the document, for example, from Krajisnik that this was the priority goal. I would argue that it is clear from the discussions that occurred in that assembly session, both from references from the delegates and also from Karadzic and senior-level officials, that there was a clear desire to separate from the other two national communities and that this would involve resettlement within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the second strategic goal, and if you can go back to the minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second strategic goal, it seems to me, is a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. "That is something for which we may be forced to sacrifice something here and there, but it is of the utmost strategic importance for the Serbian people, because it integrates the Serbian lands, not only of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, but Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina with Serbia and the Serbian Krajina with Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia. "So that is a very important strategic goal which we have to achieve, because there will be no Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, Serbian Krajina, or alliance of Serbian states if we do not secure that corridor, which will integrate us and give us unimpeded flow from one part of our state to another."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, going back to your slide, can you indicate approximately the geographical area that's being referred to in this part of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In essence, if you look to the slide, the starred area of number 2, both to the left and right of that was the territory that they were referring to. This area had been -- or control of this area had been taken by the Croats earlier, I believe in late March 1992, and there was a severance of the link between the Krajina area to the left of the slide and the area to the right, and Karadzic indicated that the re-establishment of this link was of strategic importance. But it wasn't simply that it -- from this statement here, that it unified the Krajina with the other areas, Bosnian Serb areas, in Bosnia but that it unified and linked the Serb areas within Croatia with the Serb areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also the Serb areas in Bosnia with Serbia. In essence, the corridor was important and control of the corridor was important because, as Karadzic puts it, it unifies the Serb lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Linking that goal specifically to the military, is there any manifestation on the ground of the implementation of that strategic goal by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. One of the most -- the clearest manifestation, only a matter of weeks after the 16th assembly session on the 12th of May, the 1st Krajina Corps launched operation corridor 92 in late June, and by early July the corridor had been -- a corridor had been re-established, and the corps spent the summer expanding that corridor link, and the corridor link was never severed in the war. And for me this is particularly important because the articulation of the strategic goal number 2 was clearly implemented very quickly by the 1st Krajina Corps, and in fact elements of another corps, only a matter of weeks after the announcement of those strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May I go back to the document on the ELMO, and if you could please identify for us within the text the third strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The third strategic goal is to establish a corridor in the Drina Valley, that is, elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds. We are on both sides of the Drina and our strategic interest and our Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 8555 to 8564. living space are there. We now see a possibility for some Muslim municipalities to be set up along the Drina as enclaves in order for them to achieve their rights, but that belt along the Drina must basically belong to Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. As much as it is strategically useful for us in a positive way, it helps us by damaging the interests of our enemy in establishing a corridor which would connect them to the Muslim international and render this area permanently unstable."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, can you identify that area on your slide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That area is in essence to the north of star number 3, and in the area of the box number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Drina River Valley essentially constitutes a national border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia proper; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: During the time period that we are looking at, 1992, is there any evidence of military implementation of that particular strategic objective on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later in 1992 I believe there were operations by the VRS as a result of directives that came from the Main Staff in relation to operations in the Drina Valley, but it is not addressed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, going back to strategic objective 4, and if again we can look at that in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The 4th strategic goal is the establishment of the border on the Una and Neretva Rivers."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we go back to the slide, if you can just indicate where that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've just highlighted generally where those rivers are. I believe that this strategic goal was in essence marking out the territory and the boundaries of the territory by which the Bosnian Serbs wished to control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, going back to the minutes and fifth strategic objective, if you could read that out for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The fifth strategic goal is the division of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Sarajevo, of course, is a matter that is not addressed within your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the last strategic objective, number 6, if you could read that from the minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The sixth strategic goal is the access of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the sea."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And again that matter is not addressed in your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you've highlighted a section. If it could be moved back.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We see, Your Honours, the sixth strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could read out this portion that you've highlighted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "All these six strategic goals, of course, according to the hierarchy, and that we shall finally (original underlined) -- finally finish the job of the freedom struggle of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How do you interpret that in respect of the six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe from that comment and comments later in the -- I believe from Krajisnik, that it indicates the hierarchy of the strategic goals, and that the strategic goals were the political direction that was given from the senior Bosnian Serb leadership on the establishment of the Bosnian Serb state, the limits and boundaries that were to be -- of that state, and in relation to separation from the other national communities and the discussions that were held at the meeting, the nature of that state, and that that state would involve the resettlement of people within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the top priority amongst those strategic objectives, from these minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Strategic goal number 1, separation from the other two national communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the Honourable President earlier made reference to these minutes in respect to the formation of the Bosnian Serb army, and what I would like to do is very briefly direct you to page 60, pages 59 and 60 of the English translation of these minutes, Prosecutor's Exhibit 141. Do you have that in front of you, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it possible for you to read out the ERN number? I know there are two translation versions of this. So I have one, which is page 60, is 00913560.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same version that I have in front of me. And if you could have pages 59 and 60. And here I'm referring to the numbers at the bottom of the page of the translation rather than the ERN numbers. Now, first of all, Mr. Brown - and it's a significant section of these minutes. I'm not going to take you all the way through it. But Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic speak at this assembly session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He gave a rather lengthy speech at the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And in essence, in summary, what was that speech about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to some extent not the easiest speech to follow, but he on the one hand accepted the position of the commander of the new Serb army and talked about some military issues relating to that, but he also cautioned or uttered some words of caution to the SDS leadership about what had been discussed earlier on and in relation -- in particular in relation to the issue of resettlement, and cautioned the delegates that what they might be heading down -- or the line that they might be heading down would be genocide, and it's a word he himself used. He also used a phrase saying that, in essence, what we are doing here must be guarded as our closest secret. So on the one hand he uttered words of some caution, and I think from reading the text he's one of the few who, interestingly, does utter some cautionary comments. However, he accepts the position, talks about the establishment of the army and how it should function, and those are some of the issues that he discussed during his speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, you'll find that speech, I think, between pages 37 and 50 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, specifically the formation of the army, I'm not sure if you've found anything different to me, but this is what I've found, where this seems to be a formal resolution by Mr. Krajisnik on the formation of an army, is that right, on this page, page 59?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you just read that out briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the bottom paragraph you're referring to, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think actually there's a paragraph "Participants in the discussion, article 110 shall be amended to say the Serbian Republic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] Amendments of the National Defence act so we've adopted the amendments to the constitution. Participants in the discussion. Article 110 shall be amended to say the Serbian Republic of BH has its own army consisting of standing and reserve forces. The standing forces consist of professional soldiers and conscripts doing mandatory military service. A special law shall be passed on the Serbian Republic of BH army. The 3rd amended -- sorry - the 3rd amendment, Article 11, is to be amended to say pursuant to the constitution and the law, the president of the Republic is commander of the Serbian Republic of BH army in times of peace as well as of war." Do you want to continue? And then he continues by saying: "The presidency, not the president."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to read all of this out. I think it speaks for itself. It's an existing exhibit. But are there any other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. It's not an existing exhibit. The 13th of June we admitted into evidence only some parts of this document, S141-18 to 2B and we conclude with page 57. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I should ask for the other pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you so want, then please, later on, in one package, ask for the additional pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Are there any other parts of this that you think should be relevant for consideration by the Judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Page 60 has some comments which might be relevant in relation to the Territorial Defence and the establishment of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So that is the basis, these minutes are the basis on which you conclude that at this particular meeting, the Serbian army was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now, Mr. Brown, we could move to the next exhibit, please. If we could move now -- perfect. Now, this particular slide is entitled "Weapon deadline implementation in Prijedor." Now, I know we're going to use every document that's referred to here but if you can just broadly explain what this slide represents before we, as it were, travel through every one of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in reviewing the material, and especially in April and May 1992, I believe there were some preparations, some significant preparations, made by the Bosnian Serb authorities, in essence, in preparing for war.
